title: Development and experimental implementation of noise characterisation techniques on a superconducting quantum processor
authors: Nelson M. M. Fernández, Francesco Grieco, Hetta Vappula, Stefano Mangini, Boris Sokolov, Elsi-Mari Borrelli, Matteo A. C. Rossi, Sergey N. Filippov, N. Walter Talarico
abstract: Noise characterisation not only enables error mitigation but also provides valuable information about the intrinsic performance of a quantum device, identifying dominant error contributions and bounding noise stability well beyond the aggregated calibration data. Deploying such methods on a specific hardware topology must combine efficiency and accuracy, assess noise stability, and validate the reconstructed noise model. Here we develop and implement these methods on a superconducting processor with square-lattice topology. First, we revise the cycle-benchmarking protocol and reduce the bias arising from unlearnable degrees of freedom via a regularised cost function. Second, we extend a previously developed tensor-network tomography method to match the device layout and show how its accuracy can be improved by repeated layer execution. Both methods allow approximate sublayer noise models to be extracted from parent ones. Using noise characterisation as a tool, we map the noise structure, track drift, and validate the adequacy of the learnt noise models against experimentally observed noisy estimations in benchmark physical and chemistry circuits. These results inform further improvements in the underlying technology and provide estimates of the size of noise-mitigated circuits that the device can support.
summary: This paper details the development and experimental implementation of advanced noise characterization techniques on a superconducting quantum processor. By refining cycle benchmarking and tensor-network tomography, the authors map the noise structure, track noise drift, and validate noise models. This work is crucial for understanding hardware limitations and scaling quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical need to accurately characterize noise in superconducting quantum processors to enable effective error mitigation and establish reliable performance bounds.
main_result: The developed noise characterization methods allow for the extraction of approximate sublayer noise models, enabling the assessment of noise stability and providing estimates for the size of noise-mitigated circuits.
method: The authors revise cycle-benchmarking protocols and extend tensor-network tomography to map the noise structure, track noise drift, and validate learned models against experimental measurements.
model_or_system: The study uses a superconducting quantum processor with a square-lattice topology (VTT Q50) and models the noise using a Sparse Pauli–Lindblad (SPL) model for entangling gates.
key_observables: Single qubit readout fidelity, CZ Gate fidelity, Pauli fidelities ($f_a$), and total estimation error in benchmark circuits.
important_parameters: Noise parameter drift, circuit depth (L=15), and width (N=50) for error estimation.
main_assumptions: The noise is assumed to be Pauli noise, and the analysis involves trade-offs between the efficiency and accuracy of different noise learning protocols.
figures_summary: Figures show coupling maps, gate/readout infidelities across the processor, and decay curves comparing measured vs. predicted signal decay for various observables on different lattice sizes.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by detailing device specifications, then presenting the theory and modifications for cycle benchmarking and tensor-network tomography, followed by validation on benchmark circuits and final experimental results.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, hardware-level techniques for quantifying noise sources in superconducting qubits, which is foundational knowledge for designing fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols.

Fi- nally, all qubits are measured.
